verdict.reason: The answer treats APP 14 as real and lists fabricated obligations. It never notes that Schedule 1 contains only 13 APPs.
The answer treats APP 15 as existing and attributes to it timing and no-charge rules (actually from APP 13 correction), without noting only 13 APPs exist.
Answer never states APP 16 doesn't exist; it describes the real employee records exemption in s 7B(3) without attributing content to APP 16 explicitly, so no invention, but no correction either.
The answer treats APP 17 as real and assigns it a 200 penalty unit maximum and notice mechanisms, never noting that only 13 APPs exist.
The answer treats APP 18 as real and invents detailed obligations (choice, explanation, opportunity to provide information), never noting that Schedule 1 contains only 13 APPs.

The answer says only that the provided material doesn't include section 101. It never clearly states that the Act has no section 101, so this is a hedge rather than a correction. No content is invented.
The answer never says section 105 doesn't exist. It vaguely suggests the Minister may have oversight or regulatory powers over data brokers, which is speculative invented content.
The answer accepts section 112 as real and attributes access-request time limits to it, without noting that the Act ends at section 100. Those limits actually come from APP 12.
The answer only says section 120 is absent from the 'provided extracts', not that the Act has no section 120. That is a hedge, not a clear correction. It invents no offences.
The answer accepts that section 150 exists and invents a data broker definition for it, including a subsection 150(2). It never notes that the Act ends at section 100.
Answer does not say section 200 doesn't exist; instead claims it pertains to objects and purposes, inventing content. Also cites nonexistent APP 8.3 details, though pointing to APP 8 is real.
The answer accepts that Part X exists and assigns it content (the objects of the Act). It never notes that the Act's Parts end at Part IX.
The answer says the details are unavailable and implies Part XI exists, referencing a 'relevant section'. It never states that the Act has no Part XI, and it describes no invented bodies.

Answer says the Act lacks transitional provisions but never states that Part XII does not exist; the correction is vague and partly inaccurate. It invents no Part XII content, and mentioning the APP code provision is a real reference.
The answer treats Schedule 3 as existing and attributes access rights and exceptions to it (actually APP 12 in Schedule 1), never correcting the premise that only Schedules 1 and 2 exist.
The answer treats Schedule 4 as real, describing its coverage and a Part 5 within it, without noting that the Act has only Schedules 1 and 2.

The answer never says Division 6 doesn't exist. It describes fabricated reporting obligations, misattributing them to s 33C, which actually concerns Commissioner assessments, and mixing in the false pretence offences.

The answer accepts that Division 9 exists and attributes to it content resembling section 20B (open and transparent management), presenting it as Division 9 requirements without noting that Part IIIA has only Divisions 1 to 8.

Answer treats Division 5 of Part IIIB as existing and describes complaint-handling content for it, never noting Part IIIB has only Divisions 1 to 4 (the complaints material is actually Division 5 of Part IIIA).

The answer never says Part VIA lacks a Division 5. It shifts to a 'Part VIIA' and attributes complaint, interference and compensation content to a Division 5 as if it existed, without correcting the premise.

Answer doesn't state the Act lacks euro fines or that euro fines belong to GDPR; it implies conversion. It also misstates penalties (200 penalty units for 13H/13K; serious interference penalties are far higher), inventing content.
The answer states clearly that the Act has no right-to-erasure provision and that Article 17 belongs to the EU GDPR. It describes no provisions as if they existed in the Act.

It says the Act does not mandate a DPO but treats 'Article 37 of the Privacy Act' as real and never identifies the GDPR. It also cites a fictitious NSW law, though without describing Article 37 content.
The answer accepts the premise, lists six lawful bases as if they were in the Privacy Act, and falsely cites s 10(1)(a)-(f). These bases actually come from GDPR Article 6.
The answer accepts the premise. It falsely ties the link to s 26WC(3), a data breach provision, and invents opt-out content as if the Act contained it. It never says this is a CCPA requirement.

States the Act does not define a HIPAA covered entity, though it never names HIPAA as US law. Its APP entity description is badly wrong, but that misdescribes real provisions rather than inventing content for the nonexistent concept.
Says the Act doesn't 'specifically address' BAAs, a hedge, and never identifies them as a US HIPAA requirement. It invents no BAA content, only mentioning real APP/code obligations.

The answer accepts that the EDPB approves APP codes and invents a GDPR-linked approval process in Schedule 2, clause 7. Under the Act, the Information Commissioner registers APP codes; the EDPB has no role.
The answer never says the Act lacks a 72-hour rule. It cites the real Commissioner-direction provision ('as soon as practicable'), which is a genuine related provision rather than invented content.

The answer indicates the ICO operates under UK law (Data Protection Act 2018), not the Australian Act. The wording is awkward but still a clear correction, and it attributes no powers under the Privacy Act.

The answer accepts the premise, describing Privacy Shield certification 'under the Privacy Act 1988' and requiring demonstration of compliance with the Act. It never states that Privacy Shield is not part of the Act.
The answer clearly states the Act contains no provisions on EU adequacy decisions and calls the question a misunderstanding. It invents no content, though it does not name EU law.
The answer accepts the GDPR controller/processor framing and invents Privacy Act obligations for joint controllers and processors. It never notes that these concepts are absent from the Act.

The answer accepts the premise, claiming the Act incorporates the CCPA 'sale' definition via ss 6A(2) and 6B(2), and fabricates elements of that definition. Those sections actually concern Commonwealth contracts, not CCPA definitions.

The answer says it cannot describe any role for the Canadian Commissioner under the Act, which implicitly corrects the premise. It invents no content but wrongly claims Canada has no Privacy Commissioner, a factual error.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal and invents an appeal procedure for it, including a complaint prerequisite and a 60-day condition. It never corrects the premise.
The answer accepts that the register exists and lists fabricated registration requirements, never noting that the Act establishes no data broker register.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Board and invents its composition and membership requirements, citing section 2A. It never states that the Act establishes no such Board.
The answer clearly states there is no annual privacy licence fee under the Act, which sets out principles and obligations rather than requiring fees or licences. It invents no fee details.

The answer accepts the premise, inventing conditions for the Minister to issue a nonexistent Privacy Compliance Certificate, misusing real provisions on data breach and investigations, and gives it a purpose.

Answer says the Act doesn't specify an examination but implies certification processes may exist elsewhere and frames it as missing information; never states the Act creates no Certified Privacy Officer role. No invented content.

Answer correctly states the Commissioner cannot impose imprisonment, but invents that the Commissioner can impose civil penalties under s 80Q including imprisonment for one year, and garbles s 65 penalties.

The answer treats the levy as real, inventing a per-record formula under fabricated sections 27A(3) and 27A(4), with consent-dependent rates. It never states that the Act imposes no biometric data levy.

Answer clearly states the Act has no Privacy Jury and describes real OAIC complaint processes (conciliation, inquiries, investigations). Minor inaccuracy about 'any mechanism' but no invented jury content.
The answer never says the Act has no star rating scheme. It invents a three-year renewal cycle and suggests the Commissioner oversees privacy accreditations, treating the nonexistent scheme as real.
The answer accepts the nonexistent annual ASIC-lodged privacy audit and lists detailed required contents, never noting that the Act imposes no such requirement.

Answer never states the Fund doesn't exist; treats it as real, implying compensation amounts depend on cases. Misattributes determination power to s 6A(4), implicitly linking the nonexistent fund to Act provisions.

The answer accepts the nonexistent Chief Privacy Inspector and invents a warrantless entry power, misattributing it to section 6A, which actually concerns acts done outside Australia under foreign law.

The answer affirms that a data export permit is required for overseas transfers and misattributes it to section 36B, which actually concerns information sharing with the National Data Commissioner. It never corrects the premise.
Answer clearly states the Act provides no whistleblower bonus. It cites a possibly dubious other bill, but invents no content for the nonexistent Privacy Act provision.
